items.title: Minute-By-Minute: Inside The Shocking Assassination Attempt Of Princess Anne
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>On March 20, 1974, a lone gunman forced Princess Anne’s limousine to a halt just 400 yards from Buckingham Palace. Armed with two handguns, Ian Ball attempted to abduct the Queen's daughter for a £3 million ransom, launching a chaotic 10-minute battle that left three men wounded. Featuring declassified documents and eyewitness accounts, this documentary reveals how ordinary citizens and a brave bodyguard thwarted the most audacious royal kidnapping plot in British history, changing royal security forever.

items.title: 1949-89: The Complete Story Of The Secret Cold War Ocean Race
items.author: Timeline - World History Documentaries
items.content:
<article>During the height of the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union engaged in a classified arms race to conquer the oceans using radical aviation technology. To protect its nuclear deterrent from surprise attacks, the US Navy engineered jet-powered seaplanes like the Martin P6M Sea Master and the supersonic Convair F2Y Sea Dart. In response, Soviet engineers developed massive ground-effect "Ekranoplans," including the legendary Caspian Sea Monster. Discover the declassified history of these top-secret ocean weapons, their tragic test flights, and why this high-stakes naval race vanished into history.

items.title: NEW DISCOVERY: Royal Navy Shipwreck
items.author: History Hit
items.content:
<article>History Hit's Dan Snow dives on the incredibly well-preserved remains of the 18th-century warship. 

Complete with cannons, muskets and coils of rope, it's a discovery that's rewriting our understanding of the evolution of the Royal Navy. 

The special film sees Dan on a personal mission to restore HMS Northumberland to her rightful place in the story of the Royal Navy, as one of the most iconic and important ships, the missing link between the Mary Rose and HMS Victory. Together with a team of leading experts, he'll be investigating the ship’s construction, her pivotal role in the Royal Navy‘s search for the perfect warship, and the circumstances surrounding her tragic loss.

The Great Storm of 1703 was one of the deadliest maritime disasters in history. A night of terror that cost the lives of over 1000 sailors and thirteen of the Royal Navy’s most valuable ships. Tearing across the English Channel, swallowing ships, shattering cities, and claiming thousands of lives. Amongst the storm's casualties was Northumberland, one of the Royal Navy's most formidable warships, sunk with all hands.

Lost to the sea for over three hundred years. Shifting sands have started to reveal the broken vessel, once the pride of Her Majesty’s Fleet. But now, exposed to the elements, archaeologists are racing against time to save as much of the ship as possible before it’s gone forever.

Thanks to our partners at Historic England for granting us permission to film on the wreck site and The Historic Dockyard Chatham and Royal Maritime Museum for their support and participation.

items.title: The Miserable Reality Of Life On The Mayflower
items.author: Weird History
items.content:
<article>In 1620, the Pilgrims boarded the Mayflower and sailed across the Atlantic toward the New World. But what they endured on that voyage was far more brutal than most history books reveal. For months, the Pilgrims lived aboard a cramped wooden ship, battling storms, disease, hunger, freezing temperatures, and filthy conditions as they crossed the Atlantic to America.

In this episode of Weird History, we take a look at the harsh reality of life on the Mayflower. What did the Pilgrims eat? How did they sleep? What happened when sickness spread through the ship? And what did it take to survive the terrifying voyage that would ultimately lead to the founding of Plymouth Colony?

Do you think you could have survived the Mayflower? Let us know in the comments.

items.title: From neo-nazi to soccer coach for refugees | DW Documentary
items.author: DW Documentary
items.content:
<article>A former far-right extremist now coaches a soccer team of young refugees. As a coach and mentor, he helps them build a sense of community and settle into their new home.

Thomas Eichstätt, known to everyone as "Eichi,” used to be deeply involved in the far-right scene in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. Today, he volunteers in the small town of Torgelow as the coach of FC Pio. 
Many of the young players he coaches have fled their home countries. They face an array of challenges in their adopted country: they must find jobs, navigate a lack of acceptance, and process their experiences as refugees.
But on the field, what matters most is the moment. Soccer offers these players structure and a sense of belonging. 
Off the field, many are caught up in the difficult process of integration and are consumed by a longing for home. Whether on the field or off of it, "Eichi” is there for them. For some players, he has become an important role model.
At the same time, the soccer coach is coming to terms with his own past. "I used to be a bad person,” says Eichstätt, of his time in the far-right scene. He receives no payment for his work with FC Pio—the financially strapped municipality can’t afford to fund his efforts.
Loraine Blumenthal’s film shows how soccer and personal commitment can build bridges—even in an environment characterized by frequent political demands for deportation.

items.title: Unlocking the Brain’s Potential, with Gül Dölen
items.author: StarTalk
items.content:
<article>T-Mobile 5G Home Internet. https://T-Mobile.com/HomeInternet

Get the NEW StarTalk book, 'Lost in Space: 5,000 Facts for Navigating the Universe' on Amazon: https://amzn.to/4cCD19e

What if you could reopen your childhood brain and what do octopuses on MDMA have to do with it? Neil deGrasse Tyson and co-hosts Chuck Nice and Gary O’Reilly sit down with neuroscientist and psychedelics expert Gül Dölen, to explore the cutting edge of psychedelic science, critical periods, and what a high octopus can teach us about the human mind.

Learn about the history of psychedelics and how LSD got its start with inventor Albert Hofmann's first accidental trip on a bicycle. Why did Gul give MDMA to octopuses? Because studying a creature maximally different from humans, but capable of surprisingly similar social behaviors under the drug, strips away the accidents of evolution and reveals something fundamental about brain chemistry itself.

What is a critical period? Learn how this powerful discovery is leading to new methods of approaching mental conditions. Gul explains how every form of learning and memory is regulated by windows of sensitivity that open and then close and how the reason we are so terrible at treating brain diseases is that by the time we intervene, those windows have already shut. How can psychedelic reopening of critical periods help create therapeutic treatments? We discuss the therapeutic uses of MDMA, LSD, and ibogaine.

Is opening a critical period always a good thing, or is it opening Pandora's box? Could psychedelics help stroke patients relearn motor skills, or help people fall in love again? What is the noetic property of psychedelics? We discuss why people get a sense that they know the “real truth” after taking drugs. Finally we ask: what does the fact that a single molecule can radically alter consciousness tell us about the nature of reality itself?

items.title: Why Germany Stopped Working
items.author: Patrick Boyle
items.content:
<article>If you’re looking to upgrade your business wardrobe, I can recommend giving Tailor Store a try. Their shirts are made to your measurements, so you can create something that fits both your body and your personal style. My viewers receive 25% off their first order through my link: https://www.tailorstore.com/patrickboyle

Germany just freed up half a trillion euros to rebuild itself — and eighteen months later, the money has barely moved. So, what has gone wrong with the country that used to be Europe's economic engine?

Everyone has a favourite villain: the end of cheap Russian gas, Chinese competition, Trump's tariffs. But none of them explains why a town outside Berlin can't spend two million euros to resurface a road, even after the cash has been handed over. In this video I look at the real problem underneath Germany's economic stall — a system so built around caution and consensus that it can't move, even when it desperately needs to.

We get into the suspended debt brake and the €500 billion that won't spend, the phantom construction sites, Germany's shift from mechanical engineering to a software-driven economy it wasn't built for, the "Export World Champion" trap, and why the American alternative — pouring billions into moonshots and space-based power grids — might be the opposite pathology rather than the answer. Featuring the work and ideas of Wolfgang Münchau (Kaput), Michael Pettis, Adam Tooze, and reporting from the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, and Bloomberg.

Is Germany's decline permanent, or is the recovery already quietly underway? That's the open question — and it's not really a German question. It's just that Germany got there first.

items.title: Honoring the Dead at Ground Zero After 9/11
items.author: FRONTLINE PBS | Official
items.content:
<article>After the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks came the heartwrenching work of recovering the remains of people killed at Ground Zero.

“The people who have attended to the clean-up, and I mean the firemen and the police and the rescue workers and the crane operators and the bulldozer drivers and everyone down there trying to find some remnant that could bring some peace to a family member — every day they show up and they're on their hands and knees,” photographer Joel Meyerowitz said in the 2002 documentary “Faith and Doubt at Ground Zero.”

In this video drawn from the film, Meyerowitz reflects on witnessing these first responders paying tribute to the dead.</article>

items.title: The truth behind the millennial "midlife crisis" | The Gray Area
items.author: Vox
items.content:
<article>Is "adulthood" a moving target? For millennials, hitting the milestones of the past—homeownership, secure careers, and financial independence—feels tougher  than ever. We aren't just having our individual midlife crises; we are simultaneously navigating an economic, cultural, and existential crisis, too.

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

Guest host Jonquilyn Hill sits down with Amil Niazi, columnist at The Cut, to explore why this stage of life feels so precarious. From the domino effect of the 2008 financial crisis and the collapse of the traditional career path, to the pressures of the "sandwich generation" — caretaking for both children and aging parents — we break down why the millennial experience is fundamentally different from generations past.
